applive.title: App Live
applive.summary: App Live: a session a person opens on a real Android or iOS device in their browser, which an agent takes over and drives step by step while they watch. The account side lists the devices the account can use, says which private devices are free, uploads and lists the apps App Live installs, and lists the sessions launched with a reference — waiting for a just-launched one to come up. The session side is the same surface as mobile device control: find elements and read their text, position and attributes, tap, type, swipe, screenshot, press keys, rotate, switch between the native app and a web view. Apps are opened and closed by the user from the dashboard: the device's own Appium is older than App Automate's and lacks the app lifecycle commands. Sessions are started by the USER, not here: the launch tool opens the dashboard with a reference, get_session waits for the device and returns its Appium endpoint, and the session is driven until it is stopped. For a session no person needs to watch, mobile device control starts one on its own. App Live keeps its own app store, separate from App Automate's. Browsers are device control, not here.

routing_family.name: device_session
routing_family.note: App Live is the session a person opens and watches in their browser; it is used when the user asks for App Live by name, when they are continuing a session they already have open, or when the account has no App Automate.

routing_terms: drive the session the user started

capabilities.name: list_devices
capabilities.intent: List the real Android and iOS devices this account can open an App Live session on, with the exact device names and OS versions the launch takes.
guidance: The device and os_version strings must reach the launch exactly as they appear here; a near miss is refused rather than substituted.
One model appears once per OS version it is offered on, so the same device name repeats across rows.

This is what the account is entitled to, not what is free right now: a listed device can be busy, and a launch on a busy device fails in the user's browser with no session to list. When list_sessions comes back empty after a launch, pick another device from this list before trying again.
There is no filtering on the wire: the whole catalogue comes back and the caller narrows it.
list_dedicated_devices is the one that says whether a device is free, and only for the team's private devices.

narrowable.note: The endpoint takes no filtering parameters, so this narrowing is applied after the call. `where` on os keeps one platform; `distinct` on device lists each model once.

200.description: Every device the account can use.

capabilities.name: list_dedicated_devices
capabilities.intent: List the team's private (dedicated) devices for App Live with whether each is free right now — use this to pick a device that will actually start.
guidance: state says whether the device can be launched on now: "available" can; "in use", "reserved", "cleaning" and "error" cannot. "reserved" means a teammate holds a reservation on it.
An empty list means the team has no private devices, not that none are free; public devices are in list_devices and carry no state.
udid identifies the physical unit; device and os_version are what the launch takes.

narrowable.note: The endpoint takes no filtering parameters, so this narrowing is applied after the call. `where` on state finds the free ones.

200.description: The team's private devices, free or not.

capabilities.name: list_sessions
capabilities.intent: List the running App Live sessions this user launched with a reference — get_session is the call to make after a launch; use this on its own to see what is running.
guidance: With mcp_ref the call WAITS: it is repeated every few seconds for up to four minutes until the launch has produced a session, then answers with at most one row, the newest under that reference. `polled.satisfied` false means the device had not started in time or the launch failed in the user's browser: say so, check the device with list_dedicated_devices or pick another from list_devices, and launch again rather than polling further.
Without mcp_ref every running session launched with a reference is listed at once. Sessions the user opened from the dashboard without a reference are never listed here.
session_id is what every session capability and stop_session take; it is also the Appium session id on the device.
app_hashed_id is the installed app's id, which is its bs:// URL without the prefix.
A session that has ended drops out of the list; there is no record to fetch afterwards.

query.name: mcp_ref
query.description: The launch reference the session was opened with: 8 to 64 letters, digits, '-' or '_'.

200.description: Running sessions launched with a reference; empty when there are none yet.

capabilities.name: get_session_appium_endpoint
capabilities.intent: The WebDriver endpoint that drives one running App Live session, as a STEP of get_session — it cannot be invoked on its own, and trying is refused as a chain step whether or not a session_id is in hand. Call get_session, which returns this with the session it waited for.
guidance: Every session capability (find_element, take_screenshot, click_element, …) takes hostname, port and path from this answer alongside session_id; it builds https://{hostname}:{port}{path} from them and sends nothing else there. Pass them exactly as returned — path keeps its trailing slash. For another Appium client the base is that same URL and the Appium session id is the App Live session id.

This answers at once. The device creates its Appium session when the endpoint's session list is first read, which can take from a second to a few minutes; the session capabilities do that read before the first command, so a direct caller using another Appium client should GET <base>sessions first and wait for it to list the session.
404 means the session has ended or belongs to another user. 422 means Appium is not offered on that device: the session can still be watched by the user, but not driven.
No credentials are needed on the endpoint itself; the session id in its path is what admits a caller, so do not share it.

path_params.name: session_id
path_params.description: The App Live session id from list_sessions.

200.description: Where the session's WebDriver endpoint is.

capabilities.name: stop_session
capabilities.intent: End a running App Live session and release the device — use this when the user is done with it, or asks for it to be closed.
guidance: This closes the session in the user's browser as well, so confirm with them before ending something they are watching.
There is no resume; another session means another launch, which reinstalls the app.
A session that has already ended answers 404, which needs no retry.

path_params.name: session_id
path_params.description: The App Live session id from list_sessions.

capabilities.name: list_apps
capabilities.intent: List the apps this user has uploaded to App Live, newest first, with their bs:// URLs — use this to reuse an uploaded app instead of uploading again.
guidance: App Live keeps its own app store. An app uploaded for App Automate (mobile device control) is not listed here and cannot be launched in App Live; upload it here as well.
No match answers 200 with a message object rather than an empty array; treat it as 'nothing here'.
This is only the calling user's own uploads; list_team_apps covers everyone on the team.
app_url is what a launch installs; app_id is the same identifier without the bs:// prefix, and is what delete takes.
custom_id is present only on apps uploaded under one.

query.name: limit
query.description: How many apps to return. A value outside 1 to 100 is clamped to the nearest bound rather than refused.

narrowable.note: The endpoint takes no filtering parameters, so this narrowing is applied after the call. `where` on custom_id or app_name finds one app; `limit: 1` takes the newest.

capabilities.name: get_apps_by_custom_id
capabilities.intent: List every App Live upload under one custom id, newest first — use this to resolve a stable app name to the bs:// URL of its latest version.
guidance: The newest upload under the id is the first row.
No match answers 200 with a message object rather than an empty array; treat it as 'nothing here'.

path_params.name: custom_id
path_params.description: The stable name the app was uploaded under.

capabilities.name: list_team_apps
capabilities.intent: List the apps everyone on the team has uploaded to App Live, newest first — use this to find an app a colleague uploaded.
guidance: App Live keeps its own app store. An app uploaded for App Automate (mobile device control) is not listed here and cannot be launched in App Live; upload it here as well.
No match answers 200 with a message object rather than an empty array; treat it as 'nothing here'.
Rows here carry no custom_id even when one was set; list_apps or get_apps_by_custom_id shows it for the caller's own uploads.

query.name: limit
query.description: How many apps to return. A value outside 1 to 100 is clamped to the nearest bound rather than refused.

narrowable.note: The endpoint takes no filtering parameters, so this narrowing is applied after the call.

200.description: The team's recent uploads, newest first.

capabilities.name: upload_app
capabilities.intent: Upload an app to App Live from a public download link and get back the bs:// URL a launch installs — use this to make a new .apk, .aab or .ipa available for a manual session.
guidance: App Live keeps its own app store. An app uploaded for App Automate (mobile device control) is not listed here and cannot be launched in App Live; upload it here as well.
The link must be https and reachable by BrowserStack without credentials; a link behind a login is refused as inaccessible on their side, not the caller's.
Pass custom_id to give the app a stable name; later uploads under the same name add a new version rather than replacing the old one, and get_apps_by_custom_id lists them.
The call does not return until BrowserStack has fetched the whole file, so a large app takes minutes.
upload_app_from_file takes an app that is on this machine instead, where the server runs beside the user. Before uploading at all, check list_apps: an earlier upload is still usable.

No package name or bundle id comes back here, and none is stored against the app: the App Live app API carries only app_name, app_version and the bs:// ids. The app lifecycle capabilities need that id, so read it off the running session rather than guessing it from the file name — get_active_app_info on iOS, get_current_app on Android — and expect a launch by a guessed id to fail as not found.

body.name: data
body.description: Where to fetch the app from, and optionally what to call it.

capabilities.name: upload_app_from_file
capabilities.intent: Upload an app that is on this machine to App Live and get back the bs:// URL a launch installs — use this when the .apk, .aab or .ipa is a local file rather than a download link.

shared: App Live keeps its own app store. An app uploaded for App Automate (mobile device control) is not listed here and cannot be launched in App Live; upload it here as well.
A large app takes minutes, because the upload does not return until the whole file has been sent.
upload_app takes a public https link instead, and list_apps reuses an app already on the account.

No package name or bundle id comes back here, and none is stored against the app: the App Live app API carries only app_name, app_version and the bs:// ids. The app lifecycle capabilities need that id, so read it off the running session rather than guessing it from the file name — get_active_app_info on iOS, get_current_app on Android — and expect a launch by a guessed id to fail as not found.
local: The file must sit inside the directory MCP_UPLOAD_BASE_DIR names. When that is not set the upload is refused and nothing is sent: tell the user to set it to the folder holding their apps and restart the server.
When it is set but the app is somewhere else, the refusal names the directory the file has to be inside. Tell the user to move it there rather than trying another path.
No part of the path may be a hidden folder, so an app under a dot-directory has to be moved out of it.
The path is checked before anything is uploaded and before the user is asked to approve, so a refusal costs nothing and means the file was never read.
remote: Cheapest route first: list_apps or list_team_apps, if the app was uploaded before.
Then upload_app, if the app sits at a public https link — the only route that needs nothing from the user.
Otherwise the user uploads it themselves from the App Live dashboard or with a multipart request to the upload endpoint, and hands back the bs:// url.

body.name: file
body.description: Path to the app on this machine, inside MCP_UPLOAD_BASE_DIR.

body.name: custom_id
body.description: Stable name for the app, reusable across versions.

capabilities.name: delete_app
capabilities.intent: Remove an uploaded app from App Live for good.
guidance: Refused here: the app is gone for everyone on the team and cannot be recovered. The user removes apps from the App Live dashboard.
Owners and admins can remove any team upload; other members only their own. Sample apps BrowserStack provides cannot be removed.

path_params.name: app_id
path_params.description: The app's id: its bs:// URL without the prefix.

capabilities.name: list_appium_sessions
capabilities.intent: The Appium session behind one App Live session, as a STEP of get_session — reading it is what makes the device create that Appium session. It cannot be invoked on its own; call get_session, which does this read and waits out the delay.
guidance: The device creates its Appium session the first time this list is read, so the call waits: it is repeated every ten seconds for up to five minutes until the list is non-empty, and `polled` says how long that took.
Until the device has caught up the proxy answers 404 "Session not found." or holds the request; both are treated as not yet.

The one row's sessionId is the App Live session id, and get_session returns it with everything else. A direct invoke to re-check that a session is still driveable is refused as a chain step: use list_sessions, which is callable and says whether the session is still running.

query.name: hostname
query.description: hostname from get_session: the proxy the session is driven at.

query.name: port
query.description: port from get_session.

query.name: path
query.description: path from get_session, exactly as returned, ending in a slash.

200.description: The Appium sessions the proxy knows for this endpoint, one when the device is up.

capabilities.name: get_session
capabilities.intent: Get a launched App Live session ready to drive, in one call: waits for the launch to produce the session, fetches its endpoint and brings its Appium session up — use this right after the launch, then pass what it returns to every session capability.
guidance: Pass the mcp_ref the launch was opened with. The call waits up to four minutes for the session to be listed and up to five more for the device's Appium session; `chain` says what each step answered and `polled` how long it waited.
The answer carries session_id, hostname, port and path: pass all four to every session capability (find_element, take_screenshot, click_element, …) exactly as returned.
If the chain stops at list_sessions with an empty wait, the launch failed in the user's browser, usually a busy device: say so, pick another device from list_devices, and launch again.
A session that has already ended is not listed, so the wait runs out; one that ends mid-chain stops the chain with a 404 at the endpoint step.

query.name: mcp_ref
query.description: The launch reference the session was opened with.

200.description: The session, its endpoint, and its Appium session id, ready to drive.

capabilities.name: get_page_source
capabilities.intent: Read the full UI tree of the screen currently shown in the app — use this to see what is on screen and choose what to tap, type into or scroll before acting.
guidance: Call get_session once after the launch and pass its session_id, hostname, port and path to every session capability; they are where the session is driven, not query parameters. The first command on a session first brings its Appium session up — the device creates it when the endpoint's session list is read — and waits for that, up to five minutes, before sending the command once; a wait is reported under `readiness`. Nothing is sent twice. Later commands answer in a second or two.

Not published: the whole tree runs to tens of kilobytes, more than a caller can read. Find the elements you need with find_element or find_elements and read them with get_element_text, get_element_rect and get_element_attribute.

path_params.name: session_id
path_params.description: The App Live session id from list_sessions.

200.description: The UI tree as an XML string.

query.name: hostname
query.description: hostname from get_session: the proxy the session is driven at.

query.name: port
query.description: port from get_session.

query.name: path
query.description: path from get_session, exactly as returned, ending in a slash.

capabilities.name: find_element
capabilities.intent: Locate one element on the current screen by id, accessibility id, XPath or UiAutomator selector — use this to get the element id that click_element and send_keys act on.
guidance: Call get_session once after the launch and pass its session_id, hostname, port and path to every session capability; they are where the session is driven, not query parameters. The first command on a session first brings its Appium session up — the device creates it when the endpoint's session list is read — and waits for that, up to five minutes, before sending the command once; a wait is reported under `readiness`. Nothing is sent twice. Later commands answer in a second or two.
The element id comes back under the W3C key value["element-6066-11e4-a52e-4f735466cecf"]; pass that string as element_id.

Locators by platform: resource-id → "id", content-desc (Android) or name (iOS) → "accessibility id", visible text → xpath such as //*[@text='Submit'] on Android or -ios predicate string label == 'Submit' on iOS. Once you hold an element, get_element_attribute reads its ids and get_element_text what it says.

No match is a 404 with error "no such element" — the screen may have changed, or the element may be off-screen and need a scroll first; find it again after the scroll. "No such element" is also the cheapest way to confirm something is NOT on screen.
"-android uiautomator" accepts a UiSelector expression, which can scroll an element into view: new UiScrollable(new UiSelector().scrollable(true)).scrollIntoView(new UiSelector().text("Checkout")).
find_elements answers the same query with a list and never a 404, which is how to ask whether something is present without treating absence as a failure.

path_params.name: session_id
path_params.description: The App Live session id from list_sessions.

body.name: value
body.description: The selector itself, interpreted according to using.

query.name: hostname
query.description: hostname from get_session: the proxy the session is driven at.

query.name: port
query.description: port from get_session.

query.name: path
query.description: path from get_session, exactly as returned, ending in a slash.

capabilities.name: click_element
capabilities.intent: Tap an element in the app — use this to press a button, open a menu item, select a list row or focus a field found with find_element.
guidance: element_id must come from find_element on the current screen; after the screen changes it is stale and fails with "stale element reference".
To tap something that has no usable locator, take the centre of a nearby element's get_element_rect and tap the coordinates with perform_actions instead.
Confirm the tap had the intended effect — a 200 only means it was delivered: find an element the new screen should carry, or read a label with get_element_text before and after.

A keyboard covers the lower part of the screen and a tap aimed underneath it lands on the keyboard while still reporting success. When the target sits low, call is_keyboard_shown and then hide_keyboard before tapping.

path_params.name: session_id
path_params.description: The App Live session id from list_sessions.

path_params.name: element_id
path_params.description: value["element-6066-11e4-a52e-4f735466cecf"] from find_element.

query.name: hostname
query.description: hostname from get_session: the proxy the session is driven at.

query.name: port
query.description: port from get_session.

query.name: path
query.description: path from get_session, exactly as returned, ending in a slash.

capabilities.name: send_keys
capabilities.intent: Type text into an input field in the app — use this to fill a search box, login form or any editable field found with find_element.
guidance: WHETHER THIS REPLACES OR APPENDS DEPENDS ON THE PLATFORM: on Android it replaces whatever the field already holds, and on iOS it appends to it. Typing twice into one iOS field therefore leaves both values joined. Read the field back with get_element_text whenever the resulting value matters.
The element must be an editable field (EditText on Android, TextField on iOS); typing into anything else fails with "invalid element state".
The on-screen keyboard may stay open afterwards and cover lower elements — check is_keyboard_shown, and compare get_element_rect of the next target with the screen's lower part, before the next tap.

clear_element empties a field, and on iOS — where this APPENDS — it is the only way to take back what is already there. It answers 200 whether or not the field changed, so read the field back with get_element_text rather than trusting the status.

The keyboard is usually left open afterwards. On Android and on an iPad, hide_keyboard closes it. On an iPhone it cannot be closed without submitting, so read hide_keyboard's guidance before planning a tap below the field.

Sending a newline closes the keyboard on iOS by pressing Return, which an app that commits on editing-ended will treat as a submit — the field resets and the value moves wherever the app sends it. The commit is the app's doing, not the newline's: dismissing the same field any other way can commit it too. See hide_keyboard.

path_params.name: session_id
path_params.description: The App Live session id from list_sessions.

body.name: text
body.description: The characters to type.

query.name: hostname
query.description: hostname from get_session: the proxy the session is driven at.

query.name: port
query.description: port from get_session.

query.description: path from get_session, exactly as returned, ending in a slash.

capabilities.name: clear_element
capabilities.intent: Empty an editable field in the app — use this before typing when the field already holds something and you need to replace rather than add to it.
guidance: Takes no parameters of its own.
CONFIRM IT ACTUALLY EMPTIED THE FIELD by reading it back with get_element_text: this endpoint can answer 200 without the field changing, and the status alone does not tell you which happened.

Needed far more on iOS than on Android: send_keys REPLACES the field's contents on Android, so clearing first is usually unnecessary there, while on iOS it APPENDS and this is the only way to take back what is already in the field.
The element must be an editable field — EditText on Android, TextField on iOS. Anything else answers "invalid element state".
The element_id must come from find_element on the current screen; after the screen changes it is stale and fails with "stale element reference".

path_params.name: session_id
path_params.description: The App Live session id from list_sessions.

path_params.name: element_id
path_params.description: Element id from find_element.

200.description: Field emptied; value is null. The null says the call was accepted, not that the field changed — read the field back to know that.

capabilities.name: perform_actions
capabilities.intent: Perform touch gestures on the device screen by coordinates — tap a point, swipe or scroll a list, long-press, or drag — using W3C pointer actions.
guidance: Coordinates are device pixels on Android and points on iOS — the space get_element_rect and get_window_rect report in; take them from there rather than from a screenshot, whose height can include the system bars.
Tap: one touch pointer with pointerMove(duration 0, x, y), pointerDown(button 0), pause(100), pointerUp(button 0).

Swipe up to scroll content down: pointerMove to a low point, pointerDown, pointerMove(duration 600) to a higher point, pointerUp. Keep the start and end inside the scrollable element's get_element_rect. For a plain scroll or swipe, scroll_gesture (Android) and scroll_view (iOS) need no coordinates at all.
Long-press: replace the pause duration with 1000 or more.
For a scroll without computing coordinates, scroll_gesture is simpler on Android and reports whether more content remains; on iOS use scroll_view; compute a swipe here only when neither fits.

To go back on an iOS screen that ignores press_back, swipe in from the left edge: a pointer sequence starting at exactly x=0 and moving right in several short steps. A single long move does not register.

path_params.name: session_id
path_params.description: The App Live session id from list_sessions.

body.name: actions
body.description: W3C input sources. For touch use one source of type "pointer" with parameters {"pointerType":"touch"} and an actions list of pointerMove / pointerDown / pause / pointerUp items.

query.name: hostname
query.description: hostname from get_session: the proxy the session is driven at.

query.name: port
query.description: port from get_session.

query.name: path
query.description: path from get_session, exactly as returned, ending in a slash.

capabilities.name: scroll_gesture
capabilities.intent: Swipe or scroll a region of the screen in a direction — use this to move through a list or page, or to swipe left and right through a carousel of cards, without working out start and end coordinates yourself.
guidance: ANDROID ONLY. On iOS this is a 405 "unknown method"; scroll_view is the iOS counterpart.

The returned value is true when the view can still scroll further in that direction and false when it cannot — but the FIRST scroll of a freshly opened list can answer false while the screen moved and more content followed, so treat false as a hint and confirm by finding the element you expect before deciding you are at the end.

A HORIZONTAL SWIPE IS THE SAME CALL with direction left or right: a rectangle covering the carousel's band of the screen, taken from get_window_rect, is enough — no element bounds are needed, and perform_actions is the harder way to do the same thing. DIRECTION NAMES WHERE THE CONTENT COMES FROM, as with a list: down brings what is below into view (the finger moves up), so right brings the NEXT card and left the previous one.
The area is a rectangle in screen pixels — get_window_rect gives the screen size to base it on — and percent is how far to scroll within it, 0 to 1.

path_params.name: session_id
path_params.description: The App Live session id from list_sessions.

body.name: args
body.description: Exactly one object: the rectangle to scroll inside, the direction (up, down, left or right), and how far.

200.description: Command result; its shape depends on the command.

capabilities.name: scroll_view
capabilities.intent: Swipe or scroll a scrollable view on iOS in a direction, or until a named element is visible — use this to move through a list or a long screen, or to swipe left and right through a carousel.
guidance: iOS ONLY, and the counterpart of scroll_gesture. On Android the same command exists with a different shape and answers 400 "invalid argument" naming strategy and selector as missing; use scroll_gesture there.

Scroll by direction with {"direction":"down"}, or stop when something comes into view with {"predicateString":"name == 'Submit'", "toVisible": true} — the second is the reliable way to reach a known control without guessing how far to go.
A HORIZONTAL SWIPE IS THE SAME CALL with direction left or right, optionally with elementId naming the carousel; no coordinates are needed.
Pass elementId in args to scroll inside that view rather than the whole screen; without one it scrolls the first scrollable view it finds, which may not be the one you meant.

Confirm the screen actually moved — find the element you were scrolling toward, or compare get_element_rect of one element before and after — since this answers 200 even on a screen with nothing scrollable: a 200 only says the gesture was delivered.

path_params.name: session_id
path_params.description: The App Live session id from list_sessions.

body.name: args
body.description: Exactly one object: a direction, or a predicateString with toVisible, optionally with elementId naming the view to scroll inside.

200.description: Command result; its shape depends on the command.

capabilities.name: dismiss_keyboard_key
capabilities.intent: Close the on-screen keyboard by pressing one of its own keys — use this on an iPhone, where the plain hide_keyboard is refused.
guidance: hide_keyboard already presses these keys on an iPhone when its plain call is refused — Done-type keys first, then Return — and reports each attempt. Call this directly to press exactly the key you choose: Return alone, or every key but Return when a submit must not happen.

The key must EXIST on that keyboard or this returns the same 400: list the keyboard's keys with find_elements using class name XCUIElementTypeKey and read each with get_element_text, then pick from the keys that are really there. An iPad carries "Hide keyboard"; an iPhone keyboard of this kind usually offers only Return.
Several candidates may be listed in one call and it costs nothing, but it still fails when the keyboard carries none of them — measured with ["Done","done","Hide keyboard","Dismiss"].
PRESSING RETURN SUBMITS. An app that commits when the field stops being edited will commit however the keyboard is closed, so check the field afterwards rather than assuming only the keyboard moved.
Confirm with is_keyboard_shown; on Android and on an iPad hide_keyboard closes it on its own.

path_params.name: session_id
path_params.description: The App Live session id from list_sessions.

body.name: args
body.description: Exactly one object whose keys field lists the key names to try, in order.

200.description: Command result; its shape depends on the command.

capabilities.name: execute_script
capabilities.intent: Run an Appium mobile command or a BrowserStack session command — scroll a list, press a hardware key, launch or close an app, or mark the session passed or failed.
guidance: Keep any executor reason to one plain line under 256 characters with no escape sequences such as newlines.
Android scroll: script "mobile: scrollGesture" with args [{"left":100,"top":500,"width":880,"height":1500,"direction":"down","percent":0.8}] — value true means more content remains below.

capabilities.name: hide_keyboard
capabilities.intent: Close the on-screen keyboard — use this when it covers a button or field you need to tap after typing.
guidance: On a plain success the response is true when a keyboard was dismissed and false when none was showing; false is not an error. A success reached through the chain below carries the key press's own null value instead.
A tap aimed at a control hidden behind the keyboard lands on the keyboard instead and reports success, so close it first rather than afterwards.

ON AN iPHONE THE PLAIN CALL IS REFUSED AND A CHAIN RUNS INSTEAD. That keyboard has no dismiss key, so the product answers 400 "Did not know how to dismiss the keyboard"; this then presses a key the keyboard actually carries — Done, Hide keyboard or Dismiss where one exists, and failing that Return. On an iPad the plain call closes it, because that keyboard carries "Hide keyboard"; on Android it closes it; neither runs the chain.

THE RESPONSE LISTS EVERY ATTEMPT WITH ITS STATUS under fallback.attempts, so read which one closed it. When the last attempt's keys include Return, Return is what was pressed — and in many apps that is a submit: a search runs, a form goes. Read the field and the screen back before assuming only the keyboard moved.

When no attempt answers 200 the keyboard stays up and the last 400 is the answer: the app offers no way to close it from outside, which a person on the phone would hit too. dismiss_keyboard_key is the same key press on its own, for trying exactly the key you choose — Return alone, or everything but Return.

GESTURES DO NOT DISMISS IT. Tapping an empty area above the keyboard returns 200 and changes nothing, and so does a drag downward over it — including one that starts well above the keyboard's top and moves through it in short steps, which is the form that works on a screen whose scroll view dismisses on drag. This app's does not, and neither gesture moved it.

WHETHER THE FIELD SURVIVES IS THE APP'S BUSINESS, NOT THE KEYBOARD'S. An app that commits on editing-ended will commit however the keyboard is dismissed — closing an iPad keyboard this way still moved the text out of the field. So do not expect any dismissal to be side-effect free; check the app's own behaviour. On Android it closes the keyboard, answers true, and leaves the field as it was.

True right after typing means the field took focus; false means the tap that was meant to focus it did not land.

capabilities.name: read_device_property
capabilities.intent: Read one Android system property from the device, such as its OS build or manufacturer — use this for details the UI does not show.
guidance: Withheld on App Live: the executor line this sends is handled by the App Automate hub, and an App Live session is driven through the device's own Appium, which has no such handler.
Android only. iOS has no adb and the call is rejected there.

Only `getprop <property>` can be expressed: the accepted form is fixed, and a command that lists apps or system state cannot be sent through this capability. A public phone is shared between customers, and commands such as `pm list packages` or `dumpsys` report what other people's sessions left behind.

BrowserStack applies its own allow-list on top of this one and accepts only some properties on a shared phone; ro.build.version.release and ro.product.manufacturer are accepted, while a bare getprop is not. A property it refuses comes back as an execution failure rather than an empty value.
The device name and OS version are already in the session record, so list_sessions answers those without this.
The whole line must be sent exactly as shown, with no extra spaces: it is matched against a fixed form.

The allowed property list is narrow and locale is not on it: getprop persist.sys.locale and getprop ro.product.locale both come back HTTP 500, "BROWSERSTACK_UNSUPPORTED_ADB_SHELL_COMMAND ... is not supported on BrowserStack currently". ro.build.version.release and ro.product.manufacturer do work, so treat the refusal as a per-property allow-list rather than a broken capability.

capabilities.name: find_elements
capabilities.intent: Find every element matching a selector — use this to count matches, work through a list, or check whether something is present at all.
guidance: Call get_session once after the launch and pass its session_id, hostname, port and path to every session capability; they are where the session is driven, not query parameters. The first command on a session first brings its Appium session up — the device creates it when the endpoint's session list is read — and waits for that, up to five minutes, before sending the command once; a wait is reported under `readiness`. Nothing is sent twice. Later commands answer in a second or two.
No match is an EMPTY LIST and a 200, where find_element answers 404. That makes this the way to test whether something is there without handling an error.

An empty list can be trusted to mean absent: a strategy this surface does not accept is refused before the request is sent, and an iOS strategy aimed at an Android screen comes back as a 400 "invalid selector" rather than as nothing found.
Each entry carries the same element-6066-11e4-a52e-4f735466cecf key as find_element, and the ids go stale when the screen changes just as readily.
The order is the UI tree's own, so it follows the screen's layout rather than anything meaningful to the app.
Use find_element when exactly one match is expected: its 404 says plainly that the screen is not what you thought.

capabilities.intent: Read the visible text of an element on the screen — use this to check a label, a title, a price, a field's current contents or an error message without reading the whole screen.
guidance: THIS IS HOW TO READ THE SCREEN: find_element gives the id, this gives what it says — one line per call, nothing to wade through.

On Android it is the text of the view; a container answers with an empty string, not its children's text, so aim at the TextView itself (class name android.widget.TextView, or the element by its own text).
On iOS it is the element's label or value — a text field answers with what it currently holds, or its placeholder when empty.
To confirm an action did something, read the same element before and after, or find the text you expect with find_element by text and treat "no such element" as the answer.

app_live_session.title: App Live Session
app_live_session.description: A device session a person opened from the App Live dashboard, which an agent can list, drive through Appium and stop while it runs.
app_live_session.id_convention: session_id is a 40-character hex string from list_sessions, and is also the Appium session id on the device. element_id is an opaque string from find_element, valid only until the screen changes.
key_facts: A session is started by the user in their browser, from a launch that carries a reference; nothing here starts one, and only sessions launched with a reference are listed.
Driving a session needs its endpoint: get_session answers with the session id and the hostname, port and path that every session capability takes.
The user keeps watching and can keep touching the device while an agent drives it, so every action is visible to them as it happens.
The device creates its Appium session when the endpoint's session list is first read, which can take from a second to a few minutes; the first command on a session waits for that before being sent.
Actions are decided from the UI tree: find elements, act, then find again to confirm the effect.
A session ends when it is stopped here, when the user closes it, or after the idle timeout; once ended it cannot be resumed and leaves no record to fetch.

device.title: Device
device.description: A real phone or tablet model in the BrowserStack cloud, identified by its name and OS version, that an App Live session runs on.
device.id_convention: A device is addressed by its name and OS version as two strings, exactly as the device list spells them; there is no numeric id. A private device also carries a udid for the physical unit.
key_facts: Public devices are shared with other customers and are taken for the length of a session, so one can be busy even though the account is entitled to it, and the public catalogue does not say which.
Private (dedicated) devices belong to the team and report whether they are free right now.
A launch on a busy device fails in the user's browser and produces no session to list.

app.title: App
app.description: An app binary uploaded to App Live, addressed by a bs:// URL, that the dashboard installs on the device when a session is launched.
app.id_convention: app_url is a bs:// URL of 40 hex characters; app_id and app_hashed_id are that same hex without the prefix. A custom_id is a name chosen at upload that resolves to the newest upload under it.
key_facts: App Live's store is separate from App Automate's: an app uploaded for one is not available to the other.
Uploading under a custom id that already exists adds another version rather than replacing the old one, and both stay listed.
An app uploaded by one person is visible to the whole team, and owners and admins can remove any of them.
